name: Oedipus
desc: The stranger from Corinth who solved the Sphinx's riddle and was given the throne and the widowed queen. He opens an inquiry into the murder of the last king, Laius, and pursues it past every warning until it proves him Laius' killer and Laius' son. He then blinds himself.
why: I read him as a good and formidable man whose virtues, quickness, thoroughness and a refusal to leave a question alone, are the instruments of his ruin. The play is his investigation of himself.

name: Jocasta
role: Queen of Thebes, wife of Oedipus, widow of Laius
desc: Creon's sister, who years ago gave up her infant son to be exposed because of an oracle. She tries to calm Oedipus by proving that oracles fail, and in doing so hands him the clue of the three roads. She grasps the whole truth before he does, begs him to stop, and hangs herself.
why: She is the play's sceptic, and her scepticism is grief. Her long silence in the Third Episode is the moment the truth first lands on anyone.

name: Creon
desc: He brings the oracle from Delphi, is accused by Oedipus of plotting with Teiresias to seize the throne, and defends himself with cool logic. At the end he is ruler of Thebes and decides what happens to the blinded king and his daughters.
why: He is the measure of ordinary prudence beside Oedipus: correct, cautious and smaller. The reversal of power between them frames the play.

name: Antigone and Ismene
desc: Two young girls, silent in this play, led out to their father in the last scene. He holds them, foresees the shame they will inherit, and entrusts them to Creon.
why: They turn the catastrophe from an idea into a family. His fear for them is the most ordinary and most painful thing he says.

name: Teiresias
desc: The old seer of Thebes, summoned to name the murderer. He tries to keep silent, is goaded into speech, and tells Oedipus the entire truth in the first third of the play. He is not believed.
why: He sets the terms of the play's imagery, the blind man who sees against the sighted man who does not. He also shows that being told the truth is not the same as knowing it.

name: Messenger from Corinth
role: An old shepherd, bringer of news
desc: He arrives to report that King Polybus is dead and Oedipus is wanted as king in Corinth. To relieve Oedipus of his fear of the oracle, he reveals that Polybus was not his father: he himself received the baby on Mount Cithaeron and carried it to Corinth.
why: A cheerful man hoping for a tip, and the clearest case of the play's rule that kindness and good news do the damage.

name: Herdsman of Laius
role: An old slave of the royal house
desc: The one survivor of the attack on Laius and, long before, the servant ordered to expose the royal infant, whom he gave away out of pity. He has hidden in the hill pastures since Oedipus took the throne. Under threat of torture he confirms whose child it was.
why: He holds both halves of the secret, the murder and the birth. His pity for a baby is the hinge of the whole story.

name: Priest of Zeus
desc: He leads the children and old men who sit at the palace altar in the opening scene. He describes the plague and appeals to Oedipus as the first of men and the city's former saviour.
why: He fixes the height Oedipus falls from, and names in advance the epitaph the play goes on to write.

name: Chorus of Theban Elders
desc: They enter after the prologue and stay to the end, singing between the scenes and sometimes speaking in them. They are loyal to Oedipus, anxious for the gods, and they try more than once to slow the quarrel and the inquiry.
why: They are the nearest thing to us on stage: they hear everything, believe what decent people would believe, and are wrong until the end. Their odes track the city's trust as it strains and turns to mourning.

name: Second Messenger
desc: He comes out of the house to report what happened inside: Jocasta's suicide and Oedipus' self-blinding with the pins of her dress.
why: The violence reaches us only through him, including his admission of what he could not see.
